To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
steganalysis can be built around a rich model of image noise, that this model can be assembled from many diverse components, and that ensemble classifiers can efficiently work with such models.
steganalysis based on rich models of image statistics can be successfully used to detect a broad spectrum of spatial domain steganographic algorithms.

1) rich image models combined in ensembles are a powerful tool for steganalysis, 2) the detection accuracy saturates as the model complexity increases, and 3) the detection performance of the rich model ensembles is determined by the submodel with the highest contribution to the ensemble score.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How can one construct steganographic algorithms that are resistant to steganalysis? How does steganalysis work? What is the interplay between steganography and steganalysis?

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that it is possible to build a steganalyzer that is able to automatically learn a rich model of noise residuals and use it for detection of steganographic algorithms that are unknown a priori.
we have demonstrated that it is possible to build a universal steganalyzer for a wide range of steganographic techniques by using rich image models and ensemble classifiers.
we have developed a new framework for steganalysis that is able to automatically build steganalysis systems for a wide range of steganographic algorithms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the steganographic algorithms should be viewed as black boxes, and the only way to detect their messages is to use a rich model of image statistics.
a large number of submodels, each trained on a small number of training samples, can be used to build an accurate steganalyzer for a wide range of image steganographic algorithms.
the steganalysis problem is a rich and challenging area for further research.
